system:
You are an experienced litigator who has supervised many document reviews. You
are asked to estimate, item by item, how hard it is for a human reviewer to
check one call, and to say why.

### The reviewer's task

The reviewer is law-trained but not a specialist in the case's industry, and
**has already read and understood this case**: the opinion, the contracts, and
every court defect — each provision the court construed, and for each one every
distinct defect the court construed in it, with the passage of the opinion it
comes from.

They are now given a list of **items**. Each item is one description of a
defect, written by someone else about one provision the court construed, and
the call a first reader made on it. The call is one of two kinds:

- **A match.** The first reader said the description names one particular court
  defect on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether it does — whether
  the description and that court defect are about the same words and the same
  problem with them — and not some other court defect, or none.
- **No match.** The first reader said the description names none of the court
  defects on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether that is right —
  whether the description fails to name each one of them.

You are judging **how hard it is to reach that decision** for each item. Not
whether the first reader was right: do not decide that, and do not let a view
on it set the difficulty. Not how hard the case is: the reviewer already knows
the case, so count only the work this item adds.

### What does not count

- **How hard the case is.** Two items in one case can differ widely. Rate each
  item by what checking it takes on top of an understanding of the case.
- **The number of items.** Each item is rated on its own, and an item does not
  get easier or harder because there are many others.
- **Length by itself.** A long description is hard only where its length makes
  it unclear what it names.
- **How close the description is to the court defect.** A full match, a clear
  partial match and a clear mismatch are all easy to check. Difficulty is how
  hard it is to **see** how close they are, not how close they turn out to be.
- **Wording.** A description that calls the court's problem by another name —
  "indefinite" where the court said "ambiguous", "open-ended" where it said
  "unclear" — about the same words is no harder to check than one that uses
  the court's own word.
- **Distinctions the court did not draw.** Two framings of what is wrong with
  the same words — its meaning is uncertain, its reach is too broad — can be
  told apart in theory. A reviewer does not stop over that unless **the court's
  construction turned on it**: unless the court accepted one framing and
  rejected the other, or decided the case on a point one framing reaches and
  the other misses. Where the court did not, the reviewer sees the same words
  and the same kind of complaint, and confirms the call at a glance.

### How a reviewer actually checks an item

To check an item the reviewer has to settle, in turn:

1. **What the description is about** — which words, which other provision or
   document, and what it says is wrong with them;
2. **whether each thing it asserts is true** — what the contract says, what a
   term or a document is, what happened between the parties;
3. **whether that is what the court construed** — the same words, and the
   point the court's construction actually turned on;
4. **whether the call follows** — given all that, does the description name the
   matched court defect, or none of them.

An item is easy when every step is quick and the answer to each is plain. It is
hard when a step cannot be finished from the clause and the passage, or when,
with every step done, it is still not plain what the answer is.

### What makes an item easy to check

The comparison is clear-cut, whichever way it comes out:

- **One phrase, one step.** The description points at a phrase of the clause
  and says what is wrong with it in one step — this phrase is vague, this term
  is undefined — and the court construed that phrase for that reason. The
  reviewer reads the description once and confirms it against the passage.
- **Plainly different.** The description is about other words, or a different
  problem, so the mismatch is seen just as quickly.
- **Anything extra is plainly separate.** Where the description also raises a
  point about another clause, term or objection, that point is set aside at a
  glance; it does not need to be checked to decide the call.
- **Nothing to verify.** What the description asserts can be seen in the
  clause and the passage themselves.
- **The provision has one court defect**, or its court defects are clearly
  separate, so there is only one comparison to make.

An item like that takes a minute or two, and the reviewer ends confident.

### What makes an item hard to check

What makes an item hard is that **a step cannot be settled from the clause and
the passage, or the answer stays unclear once it is**. Each of these adds time,
and they compound:

- **The two sides may name the same thing differently.** The description
  refers to a document, a party, a transaction or a category of things by one
  name, and the court by another, and whether they are the same thing is a
  question of fact — about the deal, the record or the industry — that the
  reviewer has to look up before the comparison can even start.
- **The description makes claims that have to be verified.** It asserts facts
  about the contract, the parties, a court or a body, a document or the
  background, and the reviewer has to check them against the contract, the
  opinion or outside knowledge. Some may turn out to be wrong.
- **It bundles several claims about the same defect, some of them doubtful.**
  The description makes several points about the same words or the same
  dispute; some look right and some look wrong. The reviewer has to grade each
  and then decide whether the call stands on the right ones.
- **It has the right words but not the court's point.** The description is
  about the words the court construed, but misses, or misstates, a point the
  court's construction actually turned on — one the opinion relies on, not one
  a reader could merely imagine. The reviewer has to decide whether that still
  names the court defect, and even with every fact checked, careful reviewers
  can disagree.
- **Its reasoning runs over several steps.** The description reaches its defect
  through a chain — this term, read with that provision, given this fact — and
  the reviewer has to follow and test each link.
- **The defect is relational and the description has only part of it.** The
  court's defect lies in how this provision is read with another provision or
  with a separate document, and the description addresses only this one, or
  only one side of the relationship, so the reviewer has to decide how much of
  the relationship it must reach before it counts.
- **The description is vague or general.** It could be read as naming the court
  defect or as naming something near it, and the reviewer has to decide how
  much it must say before it counts.
- **Several court defects on the provision are close to one another**, so the
  description could name one, another, or more than one of them, and the
  reviewer has to tell them apart before they can check the call.

An item like that can take half an hour or more, and the reviewer may still be
unsure at the end.

### The scale

- **`difficulty`** — `easy`, `intermediate` or `hard`.
- **`score`** — an integer from 1 to 10, and use the whole range. 1–3 is easy:
  1–2 when the decision is plain at a glance, 3 when one more look is needed.
  4–6 is intermediate: a claim to verify or a framing to work through, but the
  answer is plain once that is done. 7–10 is hard: 9–10 when, with every claim
  checked, two careful reviewers could still decide it differently.
  `difficulty` and `score` must agree.
- **`estimated_minutes`** — your estimate of how long the reviewer needs to
  reach a decision on this item, given that they already understand the case.
  Count only the work this item adds.
instructions:
Work in this order.

1. **Read the court defects** in the task and the provisions they sit in, until
   you could say what each one is about in a sentence.
2. **Go through the items one at a time.** For each one, read the description,
   then the court defects on its provision, then the call, and walk the four
   steps a reviewer takes: what the description is about, whether what it
   asserts is true, whether that is what the court construed, whether the call
   follows. Note which step takes work, what that work needs — the clause, the
   rest of the contract, the opinion, outside facts — and whether its answer is
   plain once the work is done.
3. **Rate the item by how clear that comparison is** — not by how close the
   description turns out to be, not by how hard the case is, and not by whether
   you think the call is right.

Return exactly one entry per item, under its id, in the order given.

In each `reason`, give one or two sentences specific to this item: name the

#### c051 — 12.2 Tenant's Property Insurance

```
12.2 Tenant's PropertyInsurance, Tenant shall, commencing on the Commencement Date and continuing during the Lease term, keep in full force and effect an ail risk policy of insurance insuring (a) to at least eighty percent (80%) of their full replacernent value Tenant's merchandise, trade fixtures, furnishings, equipment and all other items of personal property of Tenant focated on or within the Premises; and (b) to its full replacement value, all buildings and improvements on the Premises. Such insurance may be furnished by Tenant under any blanket policy carried by it, under a separate policy therefor or through Tenant's self-insurance. Upon request by Landlord, Tenant shall provide to Landlord a certificate of insurance naming Landlord and any fee mortgagee as additional insureds and providing that the applicable insurance may not be canceled without at feast thirty (30) days wriften notice to Landlord.
```

- **d01** (risk type 1.1, scope `clause`): The requirement to keep an “all risk policy of insurance” was disputed as to whether policies covering the Premises merely as an empty building could satisfy it, a lexical scope question the court resolved by holding that the wording unambiguously required all-risk coverage.
  Opinion lines 41-45:
```
Gander Mtn. seeks dismissal of Islip’s breach of contract claim based upon its alleged failure to insure the Premises as required under Section 12 of the Lease. Gander Mtn. argues that despite its diligent efforts, it has been unable to obtain an all-risk insurance policy to cover the building and its inventory, as required under the Lease. That is, as a result of the history of major flooding events that have affected the Premises, no insurer is willing to offer such a policy. Since it was unable to purchase an all-risk policy, Gander Mtn. obtained building and property policies covering the Premises as an empty space, which Gander Mtn. argues is sufficient to fulfill its obligations under the Lease. Gander Mtn. states that Islip possesses Certificates of Insurance for these policies, and thus, Islip has no good faith basis to make this claim. Dkt. No. 10 at 12-13. Subsequent to the filing of its motion to dismiss and reply, Gander Mtn. submitted a letter to the Court stating that Gander Mtn. “learned that certain insurance coverage for the contents of its Gander Mountain store was available[.]” Dkt. No. 24. Gander Mtn. contends that this should not affect the disposition of the instant motion because, according to its interpretation, the Lease permits it to insure the Premises as an empty building. Id.
In response, Islip argues that the Lease unambiguously requires Gander Mtn. to maintain an all-risk policy. Moreover, the fact that no insurer was willing to offer such a policy on the Premises would not excuse Gander Mtn.’s performance of this obligation, as the Lease expressly permitted Gander Mtn. to self-insure. Finally, Islip argues that Gander Mtn. impermissi-bly relies on documents outside the Complaint in support of its motion to dismiss.
Section 12.2 of the Lease provides:
Tenant shall, commencing on the Commencement Date and continuing during the Lease term, keep in full force and effect an all risk policy of insurance insuring (a) to at least eighty percent (80%) of their full replacement value Tenant’s merchandise, trade fixtures, furnishings, equipment and all other items of personal property of Tenant located on or within the Premises; and (b) to its full replacement value, all buildings and improvements on the Premises. Such insurance may be furnished by Tenant under any blanket policy carried by it, under a separate policy therefor or through Tenant’s self-insurance ....
Dkt. No. 1-1 § 12.2. This language unambiguously obligates Gander Mtn. to maintain an all-risk insurance policy on the Premises. Islip has alleged that Gander Mtn. failed to do so. At this stage of the litigation, Islip’s allegations are sufficient to survive a motion to dismiss. For the same reasons discussed above with respect to the repair and restoration claim, questions such as whether such insurance was available to Gander Mtn., whether Gander Mtn. possessed insurance sufficient to fulfill its obligations, or whether Gander Mtn. has any other valid defenses to this claim are more appropriate resolved after the factual record has been developed. As also discussed above, Gander Mtn. has informed the Court that all-risk insurance is now available to it and has publicly announced its intention to reopen the Johnson City store in April 2014. Thus, any ruling on this issue at this time would also necessarily be made on an incomplete record. Accordingly, Defendant’s motion to dismiss Plaintiffs claim for breach of contract based upon Defendant’s failure to maintain adequate insurance for the Premises is denied.
```

- **d02** (risk type 1.1, scope `clause`): The indemnity for claims arising from an “accident, injury or damage” to property was disputed as to whether its broad wording covered Islip’s attorney’s fees in this interparty litigation or only third-party claims, and the court held it clearly addressed third-party claims.
  Opinion lines 66-67:
```
Plaintiff argues that Sections 13.1.1 and 13.1.4 “expressly appl[y] to litigation between Gander and Islip.” Dkt. No. 20 at 21. First, as to Section 13.1.1, Plaintiff notes that this litigation arose out of damage to the property. Second, Plaintiff contends that Gander Mtn.’s challenge to the validity of the Lease in the case earlier dismissed by this Court constitutes a breach of a warranty under Section 13.1.4. Cf. Dkt. No. 1-1 § 20.3 (“Tenant represents and warrants to Landlord: [ ] This Lease is valid and binding upon Tenant.”). Plaintiff attempts to rebut the presumption under the law that the indemnification provision does not include attorney’s fees in an action between the parties by pointing out that there is no reference to “third-party claims” in Section 13 of the Lease. Plaintiff also claims that Section 13.1.4 cannot apply to third parties and is clearly intended to apply to claims between the contracting parties. Plaintiffs arguments are unavailing.
Upon a review of the language contained in Section 13.1.1, the Court concludes that it is not sufficient to unequivocally indicate that the parties intended to indemnify attorneys’ fees. This broad language is clearly addressed to claims made by third-parties. Despite Plaintiffs claims, the absence of the term “third-party” is not dis-positive. In fact, it is clear that at the time the parties entered into this agreement, claims made by third-parties was a substantial possibility, since the Premises would be used as a retail location for the sale of hunting and fishing equipment.
```

- **d03** (risk type 1.1, scope `contract`): The indemnity for “[a]ny breach of Tenant’s representations or warranties” was disputed as to whether it covered Islip’s attorney’s fees from Gander Mountain’s earlier challenge to the Lease’s validity or instead contemplated third-party warranty claims, and the court found no wording unequivocally referring to claims between the contracting parties.
  Opinion lines 68-71:
```
Contrary to Plaintiffs contention, the language used in Section 13.1.4 was not “unequivocally intended to permit indemnification of Islip in a dispute between Islip and Gander.” Dkt. No. 20 at 22. This language is nearly identical to the language before the New York Court of Appeals in Hooper. There, the Court found that
[t]he clause in this agreement does not contain language clearly permitting plaintiff to recover from defendant the attorney’s fees incurred in a suit against defendant. On the contrary, it is typical of those which contemplate reimbursement when the indemnitee is required to pay damages on a third-party claim. It obligates defendant to “indemnify and hold harmless plaintiff from any and all claims, damages, liabilities, costs and expenses, including reasonable counsel fees” arising out of breach of warranty claims[.] None are exclusively or unequivocally referable to claims between the parties themselves or support an inference that defendant promised to indemnify plaintiff for counsel fees in an action on the contract.
Hooper, 74 N.Y.2d at 492, 549 N.Y.S.2d 365, 548 N.E.2d 903.
Here, there is no language in the Lease which indicates an intention to treat third-party claims differently from claims between the parties, and thus, there is no indication that the Lease provides for Plaintiff’s indemnification claim. See Bourne Co. v. MPL Communications, Inc., 751 F.Supp. 55, 57 (S.D.N.Y.1990) (rejecting the plaintiff’s argument “that the language in the Agreement which refers to breach of covenants, warranties or representations in the contract can only refer to claims between the parties, and thus supports the inference that the Agreement contemplated the reimbursement of attorneys’ fees in litigation between the parties to the Agreement”). Accordingly, Defendant’s motion to dismiss Plaintiff’s claim for indemnification is granted.
```

- **d04** (risk type 1.1, scope `clause`): The provision that Landlord “shall not have any right to accelerate” rent was disputed as to whether Islip could nevertheless recover future rents or their present value by labeling them damages for Gander Mountain’s anticipatory total breach, and the court held that the wording barred recovery of future rent before it accrued.
  Opinion lines 31-33:
```
It is undisputed that the Lease does not contain a rent acceleration clause. See Dkt. No. 1-1; Dkt. No. 10 at 11; Dkt. No. 20 at 12. In fact, the Lease specifically prohibits acceleration of rents: “Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in this Lease, Landlord shall not have any right to accelerate Base Rent, Percentage Rent or Additional Rent hereunder.” Dkt. No. 1-1 § 17.1. Plaintiff attempts to argue that despite the absence of an acceleration clause in the Lease, it is nevertheless entitled to “damages” in the form of future rents (or their present value) and diminution in value of the Premises, because Defendant has committed an anticipatory breach. That is, since Gander Mtn. has informed Islip that it will no longer fulfill its obligations under the Lease, including the payment of rent, Islip claims that it is entitled to damages for total breach. Dkt. No. 21 at 12-14. Plaintiffs arguments fail to address the basis for Defendant’s motion to dismiss, which is that Plaintiff has failed to state a claim for future rents.
“Under th[e] doctrine [of anticipatory breach], if one party to a contract repudiates his duties thereunder prior to the time designated for performance and before he has received all of the consideration due him thereunder, such repudiation entitles the nonrepudiating party to claim damages for total breach.” Long Island R. Co. v. Northville Indus. Corp., 41 N.Y.2d 455, 463, 393 N.Y.S.2d 925, 362 N.E.2d 558 (1977) (citations omitted). However, “[t]he doctrine of anticipatory breach has not generally been applied to all types of contracts, its application being limited ordinarily to bilateral contracts embodying some mutual and interdependent conditions and obligations.” Id. As a result, there is a “general principle accepted in New York that, absent an acceleration clause, an aggrieved party to a contract for the payment of money in fixed installments may not, as a general matter, obtain acceleration by a claim of anticipatory breach.” AboveNet Comm’cns, Inc. v. A & D Data Corp., No. 08 Civ. 6188, 2010 WL 235005, *5 (S.D.N.Y. Jan. 19, 2010) (citations omitted); see also Long Island R. Co., 41 N.Y.2d at 465, 393 N.Y.S.2d 925, 362 N.E.2d 558 (noting that it is well settled that “no suit can be brought for future rent in the absence of a clause permitting acceleration”); id. at 464-65, 393 N.Y.S.2d 925, 362 N.E.2d 558 (discussing reasons for this principle).
Thus, where, as here “[t]here is no acceleration clause in the lease entitling [Plaintiff] to future rents upon a breach thereof!, Plaintiffs] right to future rent has not yet ripened and recovery may only be had for past due rent.” Martin v. Glenzan Associates, Inc., 75 A.D.2d 660, 426 N.Y.S.2d 347 (3rd Dept.1980). This is the issue currently before the Court, and Plaintiff has presented no authority which would convince the Court to hold otherwise. While Plaintiff may be entitled to damages other than future rents as a result of Defendant’s alleged breach, Defendant’s motion to dismiss Plaintiffs breach of contract claim for future rents is granted.
```
